Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the Allies decide that Rangers scaling the cliffs at Pointe du Hoc was the best option, versus using paratroopers dropped inland at the time of the invasion, or even glider troops?
Answer: I have visited Pointe du Hoc and I can confirm that the German gun positions are right on the edge of the cliff. Point du Hoc In addition, the positions were defended on the landward side and these defences included several belts of wire, minefields, machine guns, and trenches, as well as a couple of probable anti-aircraft guns that could be used for ground defence. The main problem with a parachute attack is that it is quite likely that many of the men would have landed in the sea and drowned. This was a problem during Operation Husky, where several hundred airborne troops drowned, and during Operation Overlord itself, where an unknown number of paratroopers died after landing in the sea or on marshy ground. Had paratroops landed further inland, they would have had to fight through the defences. During the Bruneval Raid, Operation Biting, in 1942, paratroopers were successfully landed close to the coast, but they were not landed right on top of the objective but some quarter of a mile inland. Operation Biting As a matter of interest, it appears that one or two paratroopers, from a misplaced stick of the US 101st Airborne, did end up at Point du Hoc and assisted in the fighting. Pointe du Hoc defences

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is Britain's defense plan on the eve of a Napoleonic Invasion before Trafalgar should the Royal Navy failed? Does it involve plans similar to a Fabian or Scorched Earth tactics and could it sustain them long enough for a proper counteroffensive?
Answer: At the start of the War of the Third Coalition in 1803, Napoleon assembled a second Armée d'Angleterre of around 150,000 men in a camp at Boulogne and commenced building an invasion flotilla. Inspection of the troops at Boulogne This concentration was noted by the British who took the threat seriously and went to very considerable lengths between 1803 and 1805 to build up their forces and construct fortifications. Invasion! The government raised fifty new infantry battalions for a new Reserve Army and called for volunteers. As with the LDV (Home Guard) in 1940, the response was tremendous with over 480,000 men volunteering. British view of the likely outcome The government also built fortifications in likely invasion areas, including the Martello Towers that still dot the British coastline, the Royal Military Canal, and major fortifications at Dover. Martello Tower The Royal Military Canal is built like that so that cannons can fire in enfilade down its length A British defeat Trafalgar would not have destroyed the Royal Navy, although it would have seriously weakened it, and so an invasion was very far from a sure thing. Only about a quarter of the Royal Navy’s ships of the line were present at Trafalgar and only four of her roughly one hundred and twenty frigates. Some of these were scattered at stations around the World but there would still have been a formidable number left for home defence. Even if he had managed to invade, Napoleon would have faced the same issues that confronted Hitler a hundred and thirty five years later - how to maintain an army on a hostile shore with contested command of the seas.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the Royal Navy still the second most powerful navy in the world after the US Navy? Can it destroy the Russian Navy in battle?
Answer: No. I would say that the Chinese Navy is clearly more powerful, and that the French and, possibly, Indian navies could give the Royal Navy a good run for its money. As for the Russians, we have to take into account their notorious levels of corruption and apparent incompetence, but they have a slightly bigger fleet and a lot more submarines. I think that the outcome would be very dependent on the exact circumstances and particularly on the level of participation of Russian aviation, naval and otherwise. The Royal Navy’s fleet is described as a balanced fleet, one with a broad range of assets suitable for many different tasks, rather than a fleet designed around one particular mission. Very few other nations are capable of deploying a credible carrier strike group worldwide - what is often called a blue water navy. However, as the Russians found in 1905, it’s one thing being able to steam to the far side of the world, but a whole other thing to win the battle once you get there. You have to be able to do both for a blue water capability to have any real meaning. Whilst there is no doubt in my mind that, ship for ship, the Royal Navy is probably the equal to any other navy, that, unfortunately, is not the only thing that matters. Number of ships matters, manning matters, logistics matter. The size of the Royal Navy has been reduced drastically over the last few years and, as has recently been in the news, it is having trouble manning even the small number of ships that it has left. Currently the navy has two aircraft carriers, but not sufficient aircraft and escorts for both to engage in operations. It also has seventeen other surface units, and six submarines (excluding the four boomers which are not tactical vessels). However two of the frigates, Argyll and Westminster are apparently being taken out of service due to manning shortages. Manning is a problem because of low pay and other in-service factors which lead to problems in retention. You know that something is wrong when the Royal Navy has less than 30,000 sailors but the Ministry of Defence has more than 60,000 civilian staff. All of this leaves the Royal Navy with six Type 45 destroyers and nine Type 23 frigates. Attempts to boost the size of the surface fleet, as is sometimes done, by counting essentially unarmed patrol boats and mine countermeasures vessels, are simply ridiculous. It should also be noted that one-for-one Royal Navy ships are comparatively under armed. Whilst the US Navy’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers typically have 90–96 missile cells, the Royal Navy’s latest Type 45 destroyers only have 48. This makes the Type 45s significantly less capable in any extended combat scenario. Royal Navy Type 45 Destroyer, great ships but comparatively under armed and very few in number The other major issue is logistics and I would be very surprised indeed if the Royal Navy was capable of fighting for more than a week or two before its war stocks are exhausted. If history tells us anything, it tells us firstly, that politicians are never prepared to spend the money to build up adequate war stocks and secondly, that ammunition is always expended at a far faster rate than anticipated. As an aside, it is clearly not economic to be shooting down cheap Houthi drones with Sea Viper (PAAMS) missiles costing £1.5 million each, any more than it was sensible taking out Daesh 4x4s with air-launched Brimstones. Modern munitions are complicated. Although largely unprepared, we were able to adapt rapidly in WW2, producing some fifteen thousand aircraft in the first full year of the war. How many Typhoons or Aster or Sea Ceptor missiles could we now produce in a year? If we don’t have adequate stocks of these things at the start of a war, we aren’t going to be able to simply pull more out of a hat. As we are finding in the Ukraine, and as Stalin said many years ago, quantity has a quality of its own. In my opinion, the Royal Navy simply doesn’t have the quantity, and its small numbers mean that, in a major war, it is not going to be able to withstand even fairly minor levels of attrition for very long. In the UK, the politicians have been unwilling, for generations, to fund the armed services, including the Royal Navy, at anything like an adequate level, and in this they are reflecting, presumably, the views of the public. Even with the current conflicts in the Ukraine and elsewhere in the world providing a very clear wakeup call if ever there was one, we are still actually shrinking the size of our forces whilst our politicians claim otherwise. As WW2 indicated, it’s absolutely fine to ignore the problem right up until the point that it isn’t. Then you have to pay the cost for being inadequately prepared. However, if we do grow the Royal Navy, it’s going to take time and its going to cost money, lots of money, which means that hard choices are going to have to be made - and politicians don’t like hard choices.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can British people explain? For A-level history, we learnt about British history from 1780-1928. Why did my teacher try to portray 1780 as “recent” British history whereas Americans see 1780 as ancient?
Answer: Context. I studied modern history at university and my course started in 410 AD (or CE if you are inclined that way). 410 is when the Romans departed these isles and so, in this case it is used to delineate the break between ancient (classical) and modern history. Ancient history is generally taken to cover the period between around 3400 BC (or BCE) and, in this case, 410 AD. 3400 BC marks the earliest currently known writing - Egyptian hieroglyphs and Sumerian cuneiform. Anything before that date is literally pre-historic. Nothing dating from colonial North America can technically be considered ancient although some pre-colonial archaeological remains are ancient. We can distinguish between ancient and old, and between old and recent. I would suggest that recent covers the period within living memory. What one of my history teachers (R.I.P. John King) once rather sniffily called current affairs. Therefore, I’d say that both statements are incorrect. 1780 is certainly not ancient, but it is not recent either. It is just about within the normal scope of modern. Last week, as of writing, I walked the Two Moors Way, 120 or so miles across Dartmoor and Exmoor starting on the Devon coast at Wembury and ending on the Somerset coast at Lynmouth. On the way across Dartmoor we walked through Grimspound, twenty-four late Bronze Age hut circles surrounded by a massive granite wall and dating to around 1300 BC - ancient. Dartmoor in July At one point we stayed at the New Inn in Coleford (highly recommended by the way). If you zoom in on the sign, you can see it says The New Inn since 1350 - old but not ancient. The parrot, Captain, has been there for forty years. In the 15th Century church of St. Peter, Washford Pyne - old, I noticed the Commonwealth War Graves Commission headstone of Company Sergeant Major F. A. Snowden, Machine Gun Corps, who died (of wounds I assume) in 1920 - recent (just about). As an aside, the reason it says (INF) on his headstone is presumably to differentiate him from the heavy branch of the Machine Gun Corps - the first tanks.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is Germany the sole cause of WW2?
Answer: Ah, the causes of WW2. What are causes? What, indeed, was WW2? I think that what it is safe say is that Germany was solely responsible for the outbreak of hostilities in Europe in WW2. Therefore Germany was certainly the proximate cause of WW2. That is assuming that you don’t believe, as some do, that WW2 started with the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937 (or in 1931 with the Mukden Incident according to preference). However, history unwinds backwards. Hitler didn’t wake up one morning and just decide to go to war with Poland, there are always reasons. The process was shaped by many factors, the outcome of the Russian Revolution, the terms of the Treaty of Versailles, the economic crisis of the 1930s, the rise of fascism in Germany, the cult of Hitler, the policy of appeasement by Western powers, the failure of the League of Nations, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the structure of the German economy. The list goes on and on, unwinding into the mists of the past. When considering jus ad bellum (the morality of going to war) and jus in bello (moral conduct within war) Germany failed on both counts. In initiating the conflict it demonstrated neither just cause nor last resort. Having said that, as we all know from personal experience, what is just and what is fair tends rather to be in the eye of the beholder. However, the failure of Britain and France to prevent the war is not nearly of the same moral weight as Germany’s decision to actually start the war. German troops demolish a Polish border crossing

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the most powerful battleship in history? Were any battleships ever used as aircraft carriers?
Answer: I don’t know, how do you define most powerful? The ones with the biggest guns was the Japanese battleships Yamato and Musashi with nine 18″ guns. Their likely opponents, the US Iowa-class battleships only had nine 16″ guns and rather less armour (a 16″ shell weighs 2,700 lbs whilst an 18″ shell weighs 3,219 lbs, a 19% difference). However, the Iowa had better radar and fire control and would probably be able to land more hits. The point is moot anyway, as both the Yamato and the Musashi were sunk by carrier aircraft marking an emphatic end to the dreadnought era. Most battleships carried catapult aircraft for scouting purposes, but few were used as aircraft carriers. The British Courageous-class battlecruiser, HMS Furious was converted into a hybrid aircraft carrier whilst building in 1916 and ended up with the rather bizarre configuration of having a flying off deck forward and a single 18″ gun aft. She has the distinction of being the first moving ship on which an aircraft was landed but was otherwise not a success and was eventually converted into an aircraft carrier. HMS Furious The obsolete Japanese Ise-class battleships, Ise and Hyūga were converted into hybrid aircraft carriers by removing their two after turrets and replacing them with a hangar and two catapults. These ships could launch but not recover aircraft (except for floatplanes which could be lifted aboard by crane). They could carry up to twenty-two aircraft, mostly the Yokosuka D4Y Suisei (Judy) dive bombers. The experiment was not a success. Hyūga after conversion During WW2 there was a plan to convert the Illinois (BB-65) and Kentucky (BB-66) into carriers but this came to nothing and would, anyway, have been a conversion of a battleship into a carrier rather than a battleship being used as a carrier. There were, in the 1970s and 1980s, various plans to convert the Iowa-class battleships into hybrid battlecarriers, also called the Interdiction Assault Ship, that could potentially carry a dozen AV-8B Harrier jump jets as well as a battalion of marines and hundreds of cruise missiles. These plans risked creating a jack-of-all-trades, master of none ship and ultimately came to nothing. Iowa-class battlecarrier concept - note the cruise missile silos between the ski ramps

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any instances of American pilots returning home via submarine after being shot down over enemy territory? How common was this practice?
Answer: Well, I don’t know about being returned home, you’d need to live by a river for a start. However, downed pilots were certainly rescued by submarines, placed specifically for that purpose, and, eventually, returned to the their bases. In the Pacific in WW2 US aircraft often had to fly very long distances. Damaged by fighters or flak, running short of fuel, or suffering from simple mechanical failures, it was not unusual for aircraft to have to ditch in the ocean a long way from anywhere. To attempt to assist downed pilots, allied submarines were positioned along the flight routes in what were known as Lifeguard missions. Famously, the USS Finback managed to pick up downed pilot, Lt. (jg) George Herbert Walker Bush of Torpedo Squadron 51 from the USS San Jacinto off Chichi Jima in September 1944. Future President George H.W. Bush being fished out of the Pacific During WW2 U.S. submarines rescued 504 airmen from all services and I know that British and Dutch submarines operating in the Pacific also participated in this duty. Originally the missions were primarily intended to keep bomber formations on course by picking up radio signals from submarines positioned along their route. However, aircrew rescue soon became a subsidiary mission. The first rescue was conducted by the USS Skate on October the 7th 1943 when she picked up two airmen downed off Wake Island. The airmens’ home carrier the Lexington was so grateful that they radioed to the Skate: Anything on the Lexington is yours for the asking. If it’s too big to carry away, we will cut it up into small parts The concept was later extended to the USAAF and ﬁrst rescue of a B-29 crew by a lifeguard submarine was on December the 19th 1944 when the USS Spearfish rescued seven airmen off the Bonin Islands. An interesting insight into the challenges faced by downed aircrew can be found in the following training film which is quite amusing and well worth watching (go back to the start of Part 1). Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What happens if the US dissolves NATO? Can the European countries still fight as one coalition force or will that end immediately?
Answer: As other people have pointed out, the US can’t dissolve NATO. It could, however, potentially leave NATO and this would have serious repercussions. When considering defence expenditure US defence expenditure amounts to two-thirds of all defence spending in the NATO Alliance. The rest of the NATO countries combined spend only half what the US does on defence. Of course, not all US defence spending is relevant to NATO as roughly 50% of the US Navy operates in the Pacific. The US deployment in Europe is also a fraction of its former size, but we must consider the deterrent effect and reinforcement and logistical potential that comes from US participation in the Alliance. If the US left NATO then there would be the need to significantly bolster defence spending in Europe - unless for some unfathomable reason you believe that the world has become a kinder and gentler place recently. It is difficult to assess the amount of extra spending that would be required, but it is worth noting that, in terms of defence spending per capita, the UK spends 49% of the US figure, Germany 41%, and France 36%. These three countries account for 50% of the non-US defence spending in the Alliance, but still amount to only a quarter of US defence spending. However, without US participation, the remaining NATO countries could still fight as one coalition force, albeit one lacking in certain specialised capabilities. If the US were to leave NATO, the European countries (I don’t know what Canada would do if the US departed) would have to start taking defence seriously - which could mean significant cuts to social programmes. People tend to forget that defence spending in the UK used to be much higher until the mid-1980s, so talking about meeting a 2% commitment is a pretty low bar:

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the reason for not building battleships and carriers anymore?
Answer: Clearly there is still a reason to build carriers because carriers are getting built. However, that does not mean that this will continue for ever, because it won’t. There is a reason for not building battleships anymore and that’s because there simply isn’t a use case for them. There is nothing that a battleship can do that a carrier, or to be more precise a carrier’s airwing cannot do better and at far longer range. The case for building, or not building, carriers is more interesting and more nuanced and I think that it is possible that we may be approaching the end of an era. Weapons become obsolete when other weapons are developed that can overmatch them more cheaply. The era of the battleship came to an end with the development of the torpedo and the mine and their delivery systems, the submarine and the aircraft. These are extremely cheap weapons and delivery systems when compared with the cost of a battleship. We are now clearly entering a new era, heralded by rapid advances in artificial intelligence and drones - in the sense of aircraft and ships as well as the more common sense - with networked behaviours. Taking humans out of the weapon, if not entirely out of the loop, be it a ship or an aircraft or a tank, means that weapons can become cheaper, lighter, faster, and longer ranged. Supporting humans is expensive, and without them you can build more weapons for a given cost and employ them in much more hazardous environments. In addition, the manpower, and thus the cost, required to run your armed forces will also decrease significantly, which frees up even more money for weapons. In the future, weapons may become fully autonomous or they may keep humans in the loop as with, say, the RQ-4 Global Hawk or MQ-9 Reaper. Interesting concepts under development are extenders like the MQ-28 Ghost Bat and even submarine launched drones like SULAS, and there will be many others, some of which will almost certainly have autonomous capabilities. In my opinion what this means is that, over the next decade, we are very likely to see an explosion of drone and swarm based reconnaissance platforms and weapons, including smart mines and naval drones with long range and long-term loitering capabilities. USS George Washington Carrier Strike Group, 2003 Now a US Navy carrier group is an awesome thing, but it is also a very expensive thing. The cost of a Gerald R. Ford-class carrier is around $13 billion and that doesn’t include the aircraft, escort ships, refitting cycle, or running costs. In warfare, it is a bad idea to put too many of your eggs in one basket, and having a few very expensive platforms is risky unless you are absolutely sure that they are close to invulnerable. We simply don’t know how vulnerable carriers are, because they have never been tested in a hot war. A carrier is useful because it can deploy weapons to any location within the range of its aircraft, and because, once it reaches its patrol area, it can be very responsive to rapidly evolving situations. Once the equation starts to shift, either because the carrier becomes vulnerable to new threats, or because weapons come into service that can strike the same targets as the carrier but more cheaply, then the use case for carriers disappears and so will the carriers. At some point this will happen.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the British term for "sandwich"? Are sandwiches eaten differently in Britain than in America, and if so, how do they differ (e.g., fillings)?
Answer: The British term for sandwich is, unsurprisingly, sandwich. Sandwich is a town in Kent, once England’s fourth largest port (one of the Cinque Ports) located on the Wantsum Channel but now a couple of miles inland due to the silting up of the channel. It was probably founded by the Saxons as Stonar and is located very close to the original Roman beachhead at Richborough. Sand is pretty self-explanatory, whilst wich probably comes from the Latin vicus or place. Sandwich in Kent John Montagu (1718–1792) the 4th Earl of Sandwich was, amongst other things, Postmaster General and First Lord of the Admiralty and he may also have been involved with the notorious Hellfire Club in the 1730s. Sandwich was the butt of the famous retort by Samuel Foote. When Sandwich declared "Foote, I have often wondered what catastrophe would bring you to your end; but I think, that you must either die of the pox or the halter” [Syphilis or hanging]. Foote replied "My Lord, that will depend upon one of two contingencies – whether I embrace your lordship's mistress, or your lordship's principles." However, Sandwich’s most enduring legacy is, of course, the sandwich. The popular story goes that Sandwich called for meat between slices of bread so that he was not forced to leave the gambling table to take a meal. Other gamblers saw this and began to order "the same as Sandwich", and, in this manner, the humble sandwich was born. As to fillings, you can put pretty much whatever you like between two slices of bread. I know that Tescos have produced both a lasagna sandwich and a strawberries and clotted cream sandwich (for Wimbledon), but I haven’t yet been able to verify the fabled Scotch Egg sandwich. Afternoon tea at the Ritz A little to the south of Sandwich is the tiny village of Ham which, rather serendipitously, gives rise to some amusing signposts.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which presidential son served in three wars and was awarded the Medal of Honor?
Answer: Aha! Most people would probably nominate Theodore Roosevelt Jr. (1887–1944) who was the son of Theodore (Teddy) Roosevelt, the 26th President. Theodore Roosevelt Jr. Served in WW1 and WW2. As far as I know, he only served in those two wars although, during WW2, he served in both the North African and European theatres. Aged 56, he was almost certainly the oldest man to land with the assault waves on D-Day. Theodore was awarded his Medal of Honor for rallying and directing troops on Utah Beach. Sadly, he died of a heart attack a little over a month later. For gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty on 6 June 1944, in France. After two verbal requests to accompany the leading assault elements in the Normandy invasion had been denied, Brig. Gen. Roosevelt's written request for this mission was approved and he landed with the first wave of the forces assaulting the enemy-held beaches. He repeatedly led groups from the beach, over the seawall, and established them inland. His valor, courage, and presence in the very front of the attack and his complete unconcern at being under heavy fire inspired the troops to heights of enthusiasm and self-sacrifice. Although the enemy had the beach under constant direct fire, Brig. Gen. Roosevelt moved from one locality to another, rallying men around him, directed, and personally led them against the enemy. Under his seasoned, precise, calm, and unfaltering leadership, assault troops reduced beach strongpoints and rapidly moved inland with minimum casualties. He thus contributed substantially to the successful establishment of the beachhead in France. However, James Webb Cook Hayes (1856–1934) was the son of Rutherford Birchard Hayes, the 19th President, and he was also awarded the Medal of Honor, and arguably served in five, albeit smaller, wars: the Spanish American War, the Philippine Rebellion, the Boxer Rebellion, the Russo-Japanese War (as an observer) and WW1. At any rate he was awarded the Spanish, Philippine, and China Campaign medals and the WW1 Victory Medal. James won his Medal of Honor in the Philippines in 1899 for his role in the Battle of Tangadan Pass. The President of the United States of America, in the name of Congress, takes pleasure in presenting the Medal of Honor to Lieutenant Colonel Webb Cook Hayes, United States Army, for most distinguished gallantry on 4 December 1899, while serving with 31st Infantry, U.S. Volunteers, in action at Vigan, Luzon, Philippine Islands. Lieutenant Colonel Hayes pushed through the enemy's lines alone, during the night, from the beach to the beleaguered force at Vigan, and returned the following morning to report the condition of affairs to the Navy and secure assistance.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How were the SA like compared to the SS?
Answer: The SA (Sturmabteilung) or Storm Troopers or Brownshirts (the inspiration for P.G. Wodehouse’s Black Shorts), created in 1921, were the original paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party. The SS (Schutzstaffel) or Protection Squad wasn’t created until 1925 and was, until 1929, part of the SA. An SA parade The SA was a much larger organisation than the SS and were more radical (Strasserist) than Hitler and the core leadership of the Nazi Party and believed in mass action rather than the preferred method of co-opting the political, army and industrial leadership. The leader of the SA, Ernst Röhm, openly stated that he saw the SA as the replacement of the Reichswehr (army) and the SA was growing out of control with over three million members. Röhm (SA) right and Himmler (SS) left An unholy coalition of jockeying factions in the Nazi Party, the SS, the Reichswehr, industrialists, and President Hindenburg, emerged, determined to destroy the SA and during the Night of the Long Knives on June the 30th 1934, Röhm and the senior SA leadership was arrested on the pretext of a coup plot and shot by the SS. Although the SA continued to exist, and was prominent during Kristallnacht, its power was broken and it became little more than a training organisation for the army - including the Hitlerjugend, the Hitler Youth. The members of the SA were typically of a lower class than those of the SS and the organisation was primarily more of a mass movement dedicating its time to combatting rival political organisations on the streets. They are often characterised as thugs. The SS on the other hand was a many-headed monster, incorporating the police, including the SD, the Kripo, and the Gestapo, the SS-Totenkopfverbände or concentration camp guards, Hitler’s personal guard units, and the Einsatzgruppen, the paramilitary death squads, as well as the the military Waffen-SS and peculiar groups such as the Ahnenerbe. Having said that, it was always a smaller organisation than the SA, probably never having more than 800,000 members. An SS parade The SS also developed a curious neo-pagan ideology centred around Wewelsburg castle in Westphalia which Himmler plainly intended to supplant Christian practices within the SS. The SA and the SS, two more unpleasant groups of humanity you could hardly wish for.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were any UK troops left in France after the evacuation of Dunkirk? Did all of them make it back to England before the Germans captured Paris?
Answer: Yes. Not only were there British troops left in France after the evacuation of Dunkirk but more were landed in France after the evacuation. It is often not properly understood that Dunkirk was a tactical evacuation, not a strategic one. The evacuation of Dunkirk occurred between the 26th of May and the 4th of June 1940 when British, French, and Belgian troops were cut-off after the Germans reached the sea at Abbeyville. Of the troops evacuated from Dunkirk during Operation Dynamo, 198,299 (59%) were British and 139,997 (41%) Allied, mostly French. These men were evacuated by 861 vessels of which 693 (80%) were British and 226 (33%) of the British vessels involved were sunk during the operation. Most of the evacuated French troops were repatriated from the UK to France before the Armistice, but around 3,000 stayed in the UK to form the nucleus of General de Gaulle’s Free French forces. However, the 51st Highland Division, the 1st Armoured Division, and many rear area troops were not bottled in the Dunkirk pocket, perhaps some 100,000 British troops in all. In addition, after Dunkirk, some 60,000 troops were landed in France between the 7th and 13th of June in the form of the 52nd Lowland Division and the 1st Canadian Division (I will use the term British to include any troops from the Empire or Commonwealth). Men of the 7th Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, 51st Highland Division, 6th June 1940 However, it was too late. The renewed German offensive Fall Rot (Case Red) isolated the 51st Highland Division under Major-General Fortune, in a triangular pocket between Dieppe and Le Havre in the north and Rouen in the south. With 5th and 7th Panzer Divisions moving rapidly northwards from Rouen, an improvised evacuation of the British troops was undertaken. The 51st Highland Division was eventually trapped at St Valery and some 7,000 British and 30,000 French troops were forced to surrender on the 12th of June. However, 2,137 British and 1,184 French troops were evacuated from Veules-les-Roses, and a further 11,059 from Cherbourg or Le Havre in the partially successful Operation Cycle. Between the 15th and 25th June (the Armistice was signed on the 22nd of June), 144,171 British, and 47,699 Polish, French, Czech and Belgian troops were evacuated from the French coastal ports of Cherbourg, St Malo, Brest, St Nazaire, Nantes, La Pallice, Le Verdon, Bordeaux, Bayonne and St Jean-de-Luz in Operation Aerial. It was during this operation that the RMS Lancastria was sunk by the Luftwaffe with the loss of between 4,000 and 6,500 servicemen and civilians. Paris fell on the 14th of June and so at least 144,000 British troops were still operational in France at that date, most later evacuated in Operation Aerial.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: When did they begin to train RAF pilots in Canada during WW2?
Answer: Britain, not having ideal weather to train pilots, started the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan in 1939. BCATP was part of the Empire Air Training Scheme (EATS) which also saw pilots trained in Australia, Rhodesia, and the United States. Churchill visits the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan school at RCAF Uplands, (Ottawa) Ontario, in December 1941 The first BCATP course started on April the 29th, 1940 and ended on the 5th of November 1940 when thirty-four pilots gained their wings. By the end of the war, over 50,000 pilots and another 120,000 aircrew had trained in Canada. The courses not only trained pilots but also navigators (often washed out pilots), air gunners, bomb aimers, and wireless operators. The scheme called for the training of nearly 50,000 aircrew each year, for as long as necessary: 22,000 aircrew from Great Britain, 13,000 from Canada, 11,000 from Australia and 3,300 from New Zealand. Murray Peden, a Canadian as it happens, describes the training process very well in his book A Thousand Shall Fall. I personally found it very sobering to read how many candidates died during training. Learning to fly high-performance aircraft in the 1940s was still a demanding and dangerous business. A friend and neighbour of mine, Robert Smith, now deceased, trained in Canada under the scheme and he always remembered how welcoming the Canadians were to homesick British lads. For anyone interested in the scheme, I thoroughly recommend Peden’s book: and those interested in RAF training in the United States can do no better than Jack Currie’s Wings over Georgia:

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: On WW2 B-17 equipped with H2X or Mickey radar for bombing in restricted visibility, how did the crew differ from a “standard” B-17 crew, and if extra crew members needed, what did the extra crew do?
Answer: H2X, also sometimes known as the Mickey or BTO (Bombing through overcast) set, was a derivative of the British H2S ground scanning radar. The advantage of H2S/H2X is that it allowed precision attacks to be carried out when outside the range of the standard, ground based, navigational aids such as Gee and Oboe and when the target was obscured by smoke or the weather - which it often was in the European Theatre. As such H2S/H2X was both a bombing and a navigational radar. There was a difference in usage between the RAF and the USAAF. The RAF eventually equipped most of their bombers with H2S whilst the USAAF tended to equip only pathfinder aircraft with the H2X. This reflects the difference in doctrine where the RAF bombers flew independently in a stream and therefore navigated individually whilst the USAAF bombers flew as part of a formation (box) and could, therefore, follow a navigation leader. H2S installation in a Lancaster, installed between the radio and navigation positions USAAF H2X installation in the navigator’s position of a B-17 In the RAF, because of the radar’s dual purpose, the navigator would assist the bomb aimer during the bomb run. Outside of the bomb run itself, when the bomb aimer was not manning the front turret he might also assist the navigator with general navigation tasks, including operating the H2S set to confirm landmarks for the navigator to check his position by. Therefore, in RAF usage, in the majority of aircraft no extra crew members were required to operate H2S. However, in some specialised roles, such as the Pathfinders, an extra Navigator/Radar Operator was carried. Nb. In the RAF the Pathfinders were specialised target marking squadrons belonging to No. 8 Group, the Pathfinder Force. In USAAF the term pathfinder applied to individual aircraft used to lead bomber formations. These individual aircraft were drawn from or trained by the 482nd Bombardment Group which specialised in this role. In the USAAF, a pathfinder aircraft normally carried a supplementary crew member, known as a Radar Navigator or Mickey Operator but, as the ball turret was eliminated to house the radar (except in some early conversions), the crew would presumably have remained at ten. Question: What was the reason for Germany to stop building new battleships? When did this decision take place?
Answer: The four battleships built by Germany before WW2, as is fairly well known, were the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, both laid down in 1935, and the larger Bismarck and Tirpitz, both laid down in 1936. These ships could only be constructed after the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935, as this removed the restrictions that had been imposed by the Treaty of Versailles, which had limited German replacement ships to a maximum of 10,000 tons. Tirpitz, the last German battleship The Kriegsmarine’s Plan Z, authorised by Hitler in January 1939, called for a fleet that comprised ten battleships, three battlecruisers, and four aircraft aircraft carriers, together with fifteen Panzerschiffe, basically the Deutschland-class heavy cruisers, and a large number of smaller vessels. In total, Plan Z envisaged a fleet of some two hundred and thirty warships. Taking into account the four ships already building, this meant that the Germans were committing to building an additional six H-class battleships. The design for the new H-class battleships was started in 1935 and then revised in 1936 and 1937. This resulted in the H-39 specification, an enlarged Bismarck-class ship with a displacement of 55,500 tons and a main armament of eight 40.6cm (16″) guns. By way of comparison, the Bismarck had a displacement of 41,700 tons and a main armament of eight 38cm (15″) guns. Possible photo of an H-class keel being laid Subsequent design revisions (H-41 to H-44) gradually increased the displacement of the designs to 129,000 tons with a main armament of eight 50.8cm (20″) guns, but these were nothing more than fantasy. The Kriegsmarine imaginatively named the ships H, J, K, L, M and N and orders for H and J were let in April 1939, the keels being laid down in July and September of that year. Work on the ships was suspended on the outbreak of the war as it was not expected that the ships could be completed by the end of the war. As the war progressed the Germans started to suffer from severe material shortages, especially of high-grade steel and so, in November 1941, the work that had been carried out was scrapped so that the steel could be used for other purposes, and the dockyards and their personnel freed to work on new U-boats. As well as the purely material reasons Hitler, never very interested in naval affairs, had lost patience with the Raeder and the Kriegsmarine by the end of 1942, after a series of losses and botched operations. The truth is that the Kriegsmarine’s surface fleet simply wasn’t powerful enough to perform any role that might have justified its cost. [The Führer said that] our own navy was but a copy of the British and a very poor one at that. The ships were not in operational readiness; they were lying idle in the fjords… utterly useless like so much old iron… it was now his irrevocable decision to do away with these useless ships. He would put the good personnel, the good weapons, and the armour-plating to better use. Vice-Admiral Theodore Krancke, naval liaison officer to Hitler

Question: Did Wellington consider resigning after defeating Napolean at Waterloo due to the high number of casualties?
Answer: No he didn’t and, as far as I know, nobody suggested that he should. I don’t believe that resigning was really a concept in the early 19th Century and, anyway, not many people resign after winning a major victory and huge pubic acclaim. The Observer reported: Every incident relating to the late battle is so interesting and honourable to the national character, and the source of so much commendable pride and exultation to every Englishman, and at the same time so much sought after, that we have been induced to collect them from every conceivable source and present them to our readers. But we cannot refer to these without expressing gratification that our pages are emblazoned with fresh proud records of British valour. Heaven has, indeed, smiled on the good cause of freedom and of loyalty, and victory has twined her brightest wreath to decorate the brows of Wellington. Dreadful has been the struggle, and awful indeed, the sacrifice, and even the splendid results of the 18th June have been dearly purchased at the expense of the rich blood shed on the memorable occasion; but in the successful issue of this arduous contest, we may confidently anticipate the speedy destruction of the cause of all the evils which have desolated the Continent for so many years, and the restoration of peace to Europe and the Universe, whose beams have been so sweet and transient. In any case, an analysis of major Napoleonic battles suggests that the Anglo-Allied casualty rate at Waterloo does not stand out as exceptional. Indeed, if we analyse the casualties (those killed, wounded, missing, and captured) for all sides from Waterloo, Wavre, Ligny, Austerlitz, Borodino, Jena, and Leipzig, we find that the Anglo-Allied Army at Waterloo is right in the middle of the pack suffering approximately 22% casualties which is below the French casualty rate at Waterloo, Ligny, Leipzig, and Borodino or the Allied casualty rate at Austerliz, Jena, or Borodino. Waterloo was an unusually constricted battlefield and this resulted in the appearance of a larger than usual number of casualties. Captain Johnny Kincaid of the Rifles wrote that he: had never yet heard of a battle in which everybody was killed, but this seemed likely to be an exception. Heavy casualties were noticed. In Spain, Wellington was certainly aware of the effect on public opinion at home. After Talavera, he wrote: How I shall be abused [by the government and press] for our loss [of men]…I was hit but not hurt and I had my coat shot through. Almost all the staff officers are wounded or have had their horses shot. Never was there such a murderous battle! and later in the Peninsular he made another reference to public sensibilities: This becomes doubly necessary as I see that notwithstanding the fondness of the British nation for the sport, and their exultation upon our success, they began to cry out the other day upon the loss of 300 or 400 men the unsuccessful storm of San Sebastián. However, Wellington was careful to try to deploy his men in such a way as to minimise casualties, although whether this was out of a particular concern for the men or simply good battle management cannot be discerned. Whichever is true, he was keenly aware of the consequences of battle: Well, thank God, I don’t know what it is to lose a battle; but certainly nothing can be more painful than to gain one with the loss of so many friends. After Waterloo, he is reported as being: much affected. I felt his tears dropping fast on my hands, and looking towards him, saw them chasing one another in furrows over his dusty cheeks. However, I should note that this may be because of the loss of senior officers, friends and aides-de-camp rather than the ordinary troops; it is impossible to tell. When Wellington left the battlefield he was utterly exhausted. It is said that he wept as he was told of the terrible losses and said: I hope to God I have fought my last battle. He had.

Question: How many ships were in the British and U.S. navies during the Napoleonic Wars? Was there a significant difference in the number of ships between the two sides?
Answer: The Napoleonic Wars lasted from 1803 to 1815. When the Continental Navy was disbanded it had eleven ships remaining of the approximately sixty-five that had served at some point. The last ship in the Continental Navy, the frigate Alliance was sold out of service for $26,000 on the 1st of August 1785. After 1785, the United States effectively had no navy until 1797 when the heavy frigates United States, Constellation, and Constitution came into service following the Naval Act of 1794. In the War of 1812, the US Navy had no ships of the line and of their sixteen ships only nine were frigates, including the heavy frigates Chesapeake, Congress, Constellation, Constitution, United States, and President, the rest being brigs, sloops, and schooners. The Independence, a 74-gun ship, was launched at Charlestown, Massachusetts, in June 1814, while, four months later, the Washington, another 74-gun ship, was completed at Portsmouth. USS Franklin 74, commissioned in 1817 In 1816, after the Napoleonic Wars had ended, Congress provided for a million dollars a year for six years to build nine 74-gun ships of the line, twelve 44-gun frigates and three steam-propelled batteries for harbour defence. However, these ambitions were later scaled back and only four and two, respectively, had been launched by 1826. In 1815, the Royal Navy had around 150 ships of the line and 180 frigates and, taking into account other smaller vessels, the total size of the fleet probably exceeded 500 vessels. However, fairly obviously, the North American station was not a priority for the Royal Navy during the Napoleonic Wars and was starved of resources as the Navy sought to contain Napoleon and maintain the Channel blockade. Therefore, the early successes of the American heavy frigates against their lighter British counterparts in the War of 1812 caused consternation in Britain and the station was rapidly reinforced. By 1813 the Royal Navy was successfully blockading New York City, Charleston, Port Royal, Savannah, and New Orleans, causing American exports to drop from $45 million in 1811 to $7 million in 1814 and largely confining the US Navy in its ports. Therefore, I think that it is fair to say that there was a pretty significant difference in size between the two navies during the Napoleonic Wars - even though the bulk of the Royal Navy was not deployed on the North American Station.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is coal necessary for an industrial revolution? If not, what alternative sources could have been used to power steam engines and factories during that time period?
Answer: No, it is not necessary, but it is very handy. It is worth noting at the outset that the industrial revolution was about far more than steam engines, it was about standardisation, specialisation and the division of labour (see Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations for example), the invention of tool making machinery (lathes for example), extensive scientific research, etc. The alternatives to coal are human power, animal power, wind power, water power, and burning wood (or peat, heather, or furze). Arkwright’s Water Frame for spinning cotton, and Cartwright’s Power Loom for weaving fabric were both powered by water. Power loom weaving, driven by shafts and belts Therefore, wind and water power can certainly be used in industrial processes, and wood was used extensively to produce steam in early-industrial America. However, wood has many other uses as well as simply burning it. You can’t build houses, or ships, or make railway ties out of coal for instance. Captain Cuthbert Collingwood, later to become an admiral and Nelson's second in command at Trafalgar, had his home at Morpeth, in Northumberland, and when he was there on half pay or on leave he loved to walk over the hills with his dog Bounce. He always started off with a handful of acorns in his pockets, and as he walked he would press an acorn into the soil whenever he saw a good place for an oak tree to grow. Some of the oaks he planted are probably still growing more than a century and a half later ready to be cut to build ships of the line at a time when nuclear submarines are patrolling the seas, because Collingwood's purpose was to make sure that the Navy would never want for oaks to build the fighting ships upon which the country's safety depended. Life in Nelson’s Navy, Dudley Pope The late Sixteenth and early Seventeenth centuries in Britain (Elizabeth I and James I) saw significant increases in the population and a soaring demand for wood for all purposes, as can be seen from the rising prices. The smelting of metals at high temperatures required huge amounts of wood to be turned into charcoal, and by 1615, we see James I issuing a ban on burning firewood for glass production by declaring that “the great waste of timber in making glass is a matter of serious concern.” Coal, readily available in Britain, was the obvious alternative. Anthracite (high grade) coal burns hotter than wood, and takes up less volume for transport and storage than wood, burns for longer, and provides more consistent heat. The hottest wood fire burns at around 1,600 degrees F, whilst anthracite burns at about 3,000 degrees F. It takes roughly two tons of bulky wood to provide the energy equivalent of one ton of more compact coal. Therefore, I think that the answer to the question is that coal is not necessary to power industrial processes but that there simply wasn’t enough wood available to meet industrial demands at the scale required. The industrial revolution could still have occurred, but it would have been much more limited in scope because of the limitations in the fuels available and its supply.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: So what is this 'Black Rod' in UK Parliament as reportedly a 'bizarre scene'? What is at stake?
Answer: The Usher of the Black Rod, commonly known as Black Rod, is an official of the House of Lords whose symbol of office is an ebony (black) staff topped by a golden lion. Black Rod is simultaneously the Usher of the Black Rod, Serjeant-at-Arms in the House of Lords, and Secretary to the Lord Great Chamberlain. Sarah Clarke, Black Rod since 2018 The office originated as Usher of the Order of the Garter. Letters of Patent were issued in 1361 by King Edward III to create the Usher as a Court position involved in meeting with Parliament. By the sixteenth century, the role had evolved to become a position entirely associated with Parliament and, in essence, Black Rod became the monarch's representative in the House of Lords. Although Black Rod has other duties, the most well known is their official role in the State Opening of Parliament. This ceremony may seem silly or bizarre, but it makes a very important point in our system of government. In 1628, after disputes with the King, Charles I, Parliament passed the Petition of Right. This provided that no person should be forced to provide a gift, loan or tax without an Act of Parliament, that no individual should be imprisoned or detained without cause, and no soldiers should be billeted in private houses without the consent of the owner. Charles, forced into a corner by his need to raise money, accepted the petition with bad grace. He then promptly dissolved Parliament in 1629, starting eleven years of rule without a parliament. In 1640 Charles again needed money to fight the Bishops’ Wars against the Covenanters in Scotland and so he summoned Parliament, dismissed it again when it refused to provide funds and then, in desperation, summoned it again after the Battle of Newburn. Parliament promptly presented to the King the Grand Remonstrance, a list of two hundred and four grievances against Charles’ foreign, financial, legal and religious policies - although carefully not couched as an accusation against the King himself but against his ministers and a supposed Catholic conspiracy. This was too much and, in January 1641, Charles sought to arrest five Members of Parliament he believed to be the ringleaders: John Hampden, Arthur Haselrig, Denzil Holles, John Pym, and William Strode. Arriving at the Commons with around eighty armed troops, Charles entered the chamber without soldiers and called for the members by name. Pre-warned, the five members had fled by river to the City of London and when Charles asked the Speaker of the House of Commons, William Lenthall, where they were, he famously, and rather bravely, replied: May it please your majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place but as this House is pleased to direct me whose servant I am here; and I humbly beg your majesty's pardon that I cannot give any other answer than this to what your majesty is pleased to demand of me. It may not seem much, but this was the first time that a Speaker had declared his allegiance to parliament rather than the monarch and it was a critical step in defining the changing relationship between the two and the independence of Parliament. It was also one of several events that led to the English Civil War and Charles’ eventual trial by Parliament and execution. At the State Opening of Parliament, after the King has been seated on the throne in the House of Lords, Black Rod is despatched to the Commons to summon MPs to hear the King’s Speech (which is, in fact, written by the Prime Minister and outlines the government’s policy). When Black Rod arrives at the Commons Chamber, the door is slammed in his or her face and Black Rod then has to bang on it three times to ask for admission. Black Rod summons the Commons In 1641, the custom, as noted in the House of Commons Journal, was ignored: Mr Maxwell, coming to the House, with a Message, without his Black Rod; and coming in, before he was called in: Exception was taken to both. The tradition has been continued as a way to symbolise the Commons' independence from both the Monarch and from the Lords. After knocking, Black Rod is admitted to the Commons chamber and requests the Members' attendance. The Members of Parliament then pair up and, led by the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition, follow – in a deliberately boisterous way to signal their independence – Black Rod to the bar of the House of Lords to hear the King's Speech. Dennis Skinner (aka the Beast of Bolsover) now retired but an MP for that constituency for forty-nine years was known for his heckling of Black Rod when he arrived at the Commons Chamber, most famously: Ey up, here comes Puss in Boots and Get your skates on, first race is half-past two. That latter in reference to the fact that the speech had been rescheduled and the Queen had missed a morning’s racing at Ascot. If you want to watch the ceremony, Black Rod’s participation starts at 3:30. If you can’t see the video you can search for Queen's Speech : Black Rod heads to Commons to summon MPs.

Question: I've read somewhere, that the armour of the Panzer 38(t) wasn't RHA. If not RHA, what was it?
Answer: RHA is the abbreviation for rolled homogeneous armour, a hot-rolling process that changes the crystalline structure of the steel, homogenising it throughout. The Pz 38(t) armour was produced at the Poldi steel works in Kladno, Czechoslovakia and had either 25mm front armour or 50mm front armour made from a pair of 25mm plates, probably because the mill could only produce plates with a maximum thickness of 25mm. It appears that the inner plate was homogenised and the outer homogenised and the cemented (carburized) - treated with carbon-bearing gases to harden the surface. Panzerkampfwagen 38(t) Ausf A The alternative to homogeneous armour was cast armour. Obviously cast armour allows any shape to be produced whilst RHA plates are generally flat but rather more durable. I think (but am happy to be corrected) that the Panzer 38(t) did have RHA armour but with a cemented face. Panzer 38(t) riveted double plate front armour

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it feasible to construct a modernized version of a dreadnought-style battleship that could withstand modern threats such as missiles and torpedoes?
Answer: Why would you want to? Dreadnoughts only had one practical purpose and that was to fight other dreadnoughts. In an evolutionary arms race against themselves, they became bigger, more heavily armed and armoured, and more expensive, until much cheaper and more flexible weapons: mines, submarines, and aircraft rendered them obsolete. Nobody would want to build a ship with big guns theses days. The biggest recent attempt, the 6″ (155m) AGS on the Zumwalt destroyers ended in a shambles. Even these guns, large by modern standards, were tiny in comparison to the 14″-18″ guns found on the later generations of battleships. The longest range naval hit in history was when HMS Warspite hit the Italian the battleship Giulio Cesare at a range of 26,000 yards (just under 15 miles). This is obviously a trivial distance for a missile, the Naval Strike Missile that will equip the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers for instance has a range of 120–160 miles. Warspite’s eight BL 15-inch Mk I naval guns each weighed over 100 tons and they were housed in four massive armoured turrets weighing over 2,000 tons each. Together with all the other gubbins, that meant that Warspite weighed in at around 40,000 tons. A Type 45 can destroy a target at ten times the range of Warspite and only weighs in at 9,500 tons. If you don’t need gigantic guns, you don’t need a gigantic ship. HMS Warspite, a Queen Elizabeth-class dreadnought HMS Diamond, a Type 45 destroyer Warspite is also a good example, because, despite her size, she was vulnerable. In 1916, she was missed by three torpedoes fired by an unknown U-Boat, and another torpedo fired by U-47 missed her in 1940. If any of those had hit, her career might have ended prematurely. She was also badly damaged by German aircraft whilst off Crete and had to sail to the US for repairs, and finally she was hit by a Fritz-X missile (actually a guided bomb) off Salerno and, again, badly damaged. A torpedo, a mine, an aircraft bomb, or a missile, can kill a battleship at a trivial cost, much as we see expensive tanks being destroyed by cheap drones in the Ukraine. The economics and the risk/reward in building them just doesn’t add up. If there is a modern justification for a large ship, it would probably be ana arsenal ship, such as was proposed by the US Navy in the 1990s. These ships need to be large because they are designed to carry hundreds of missiles. However, an even more sensible solution would be to make them submersible and thus only vulnerable to ASW assets. This is the path taken by converting some Ohio-class submarines into SSGNs armed with cruise missiles. There is no viable use case for a modern dreadnought. It couldn’t do anything better than an aircraft carrier can and it would not be proof against modern torpedoes - which are designed to break a ship’s back by exploding under them, rather than by penetrating armour - and, although it might withstand one or two missile hits, it almost certainly couldn’t withstand a determined missile attack without either becoming a mission kill or a total loss. It would also be very expensive to build and man; you’d be better off spending the money on a carrier - although they may also be on the cusp of obsolescence.

Question: Was Churchill aware of Operation Sea Lion before publicly announcing it after the attack on Pearl Harbor?
Answer: Say what? Sea Lion (Unternehmen Seelöwe) was a German operation - the planned invasion of the British Isles. It wasn’t a British operation, so there was no reason for Churchill to “announce” it. Churchill did issue instructions to the public on how to behave in the event of invasion and, of course, their is his famous beaches speech, part of which reads: Even though large tracts of Europe and many old and famous States have fallen or may fall into the grip of the Gestapo and all the odious apparatus of Nazi rule, we shall not flag or fail. We shall go on to the end. We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be. We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender. Come on Adolf - if you think you’re hard enough At any rate, the Germans abandoned Sea Lion as unachievable in September 1940, well over a year before the attack on Pearl Harbour. British Intelligence was well aware of the German preparations from photo-reconnaissance and other intelligence means, not least the German’s own propaganda broadcasts (the much derided Lord Haw Haw) and Churchill was, as a matter of course, kept informed on a daily basis. In September 1940, Hitler told an approving Berlin crowd: “And when people in England today nosily inquire: ‘Well, why isn’t he coming?’ Calm yourselves: he is coming! Curiosity killed the cat.” In October 1940, Churchill responded, “We are waiting for the long-promised invasion. So are the fishes.” Keep calm and carry on

Question: Is it true that Britain has nuclear weapons? If so, why is it not widely known or seen?
Answer: Britain has possessed nuclear weapons since 1952. That puts Britain amongst the nine states that possess acknowledged nuclear weapons: the USA, Russia, Britain, France, China, India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea. I would have thought that this fact was fairly well known. If it isn’t that might explain some of the comments from Russian posters who seem to believe that they can threaten nuclear war without retaliation. Although Britain and Canada had played a major role in the Manhattan Project, they were frozen out of the US nuclear programme by the McMahon Act (aka the Atomic Energy Act) in 1946 when the US reneged on the 1944 Hyde Park Agreement. This essentially meant that the British had to develop their own bomb again from scratch. The first weapon deployed by Britain was the Blue Danube air-dropped bomb in 1953, followed by Red Beard in 1961 and Cleo (WE.177) in the late 1960s. Britain’s first megaton bomb, Orange Herald, was tested in 1957 as was Round A, Britain’s first thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb. Blue Danube bomb being dropped by a Vickers Valiant, the first of the V-bombers The V-Bomber force reached its peak in June 1964, when 50 Valiants, 70 Vulcans and 39 Victors were in service. Victor Vulcan The 1958 US–UK Mutual Defence Agreement reopened cooperation with the USA and paved the way for the Polaris programme. As far as I know, Britain’s air-dropped bombs were withdrawn in 1998. From that point on, Britain has relied on its Polaris, and now Trident, submarine launched missiles. HMS Vanguard Trident SSBN Currently, Britain has a stockpile of around 225 nuclear warheads in the 100 kiloton range (warhead yields have been reducing as accuracy improves) that can be launched by Trident II missiles from Vanguard-class and the coming Dreadnought-class SSBNs. Although a Vanguard-class submarine can carry up to 96 warheads, they currently carry 40 on patrol. This may not seem much compared with Britain’s Cold War peak of around 520 warheads but, given improvements in accuracy, realistically no country is going to going to be able to absorb even a dozen warheads without catastrophic damage. It is worth noting that this is particularly the case in Russia where the population is highly concentrated around Moscow and St. Petersburg. This is why I find the apparent Russian media attitude towards the use of nuclear weapons so odd. People who live in glass-houses, etc.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is USA today a greater superpower than the British empire at its prime?
Answer: The British Empire. The Empire was at its greatest extent just after WW1, but it was probably in its prime in the latter half of the 19th Century. In terms of relative population there is no contest. At one time the Empire contained about 25% of the World’s population, whilst the USA only has about 4.2%. The Empire also covered getting on for 25% of the World’s land area (13.7 million square miles) whilst the USA covers about 6.5% (3.8 million square miles). Quite a lot of that land area was in Australia and Canada and didn’t have much going for it except for its potential for raw materials, but the United States also has over 100 million acres of wilderness. In its prime the Empire also controlled most of the World’s shipping, most of its industry, and a very large proportion of its banking. None of this is true of the current United States. The Royal Navy also exercised uncontested dominance of the World’s seas - something that is probably currently true of the United States. It is difficult to make comparisons across technological eras Of course, the Empire didn’t have weapons of mass destruction or any other modern gizmos, so the pace of superpower life was rather slower and the risk of immediate immolation wasn’t something that needed to be worried about. In the matter of soft and cultural power, the Hollywood factor, it is arguable that the USA has more influence today than Britain did in the past, but that is simply because such a thing didn’t exist to any extent. No television, no radio, no telephones, no movies - every nation was still wedded to its own culture and traditions to a much greater extent than is true today. In terms of cultural influence, the Empire was probably on a par with France, Germany, and Russia. A final factor to consider is that the Empire actually maintained a tiny army and so, although it could bring maritime commerce to a halt at will, it had no real ability to project serious amounts of power inland and its army was a fraction of the size of the Continental Powers. Traditionally, the USA has also maintained a very small military but, since, WW2, it has taken on more responsibilities and maintains larger armed forces than the Empire ever did in peacetime.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During WWII in the Pacific did the British army (note: not the Australians or New Zealanders) ever fight against the Japanese army in any place not part of the 1939 British Empire? If so, where and when?
Answer: The British Army, as opposed to the Royal Navy and the RAF, played no part in the Pacific Theatres as the Pacific was an American endeavour with assistance from Australia and New Zealand. Edit: Stephen Phillips points out below that the British Army, in the shape of 16 AA Brigade (6 and 77 Heavy AA Regiments and 21, 35, and 48 Light AA Regiments) supported by B Squadron of 3rd Hussars, did take part in the defence of Java in February and March 1942. Java was not part of the British Empire. In the Far East, the British and Indian Armies, as XIV Army, were occupied fighting the Japanese 15th, 28th, and 33rd Armies in the South-East Asian Theatre, generally known as the Burma Campaign. As a result, the XIV Army, nearly a million men by 1944, were fighting in Singapore, Malaya, Burma and India from 1941 to the end of the war. As far as I am aware, this fighting was all within the extent of the British Empire. The British Army was later involved in some local conflicts in the Dutch East Indies, Thailand/Siam, and Vietnam, which were not part of the British Empire, but this was immediately after the Japanese surrender.
